```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# The simulation results come from dev/rn-fp/sim/ (calibration and general
# grid) and dev/rn-fp/acad-real/ (a small design under four priors), run on
# AWS, so that the article builds without Stan.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6, out.width = "100%")
library(crywolf)
res <- readRDS("royle-nichols-results.rds")
pct <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(round(100 * x, digits), "%")
rng <- function(x) paste0(pct(min(x)), "-", pct(max(x)))
```

In `fp_occu()`, the probability of detecting the species at an occupied
site is the same function of covariates at every site. In reality, a site
with many calling individuals is detected more often than a site with one.
Variation in detection among sites then has two possible sources:
abundance, and everything else (distance to the recorder, background noise,
vegetation). `fp_occu()` with `random_det = TRUE` captures the sum of both,
but cannot tell them apart.

`fp_occu_rn()` fits the model of Royle and Nichols (2003), in which detection
depends on abundance, with the false positives and verification of
`fp_occu()`. A site effect on the per-individual detection rate then
measures the variation in detection that abundance does not explain. This
article describes the model, shows how to fit and check it, and reports
the simulations that show what it can and cannot recover. The fitting code
is shown but not run when the article is built.

## The model

The number of individuals at site \(i\) is
\(N_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i)\), with
\(\log \lambda_i = X_i \beta + v_i\). The site is occupied when
\(N_i > 0\), so the occupancy probability is \(\psi_i = 1 - e^{-\lambda_i}\).
Each individual is detected on an occasion with probability \(r\), and the
automated method detects at least one with probability
\(1 - (1 - r_{ik})^{N_i}\), where
\(\mathrm{logit}(r_{ik}) = Z_{ik} \alpha + d_i\).
False positives occur on every automated occasion with probability
\(p_{10}\), also at occupied sites. An occasion is a detection when either
a true or a false observation occurs:
\[
\Pr(y_{ik} = 1 \mid N_i) = 1 - (1 - r_{ik})^{N_i} (1 - p_{10,i}).
\]
A verified occasion has no false positives and is a detection with
probability \(1 - (1 - r^{v})^{N_i}\). The abundance \(N_i\) is summed out
of the likelihood over 0 to `n_max`.

The two site effects are the point of the model:

- \(v_i\), with standard deviation `sd_abund_site` (`random_abund = TRUE`),
  is variation in abundance beyond the covariates of `occ`.
- \(d_i\), with standard deviation `sd_det_site` (`random_det = TRUE`), is
  variation in the per-individual detection rate.

Both raise the variance of detections among occupied sites. They differ in
what else they predict. Abundance also changes the share of occupied sites
and the detection by the verified method. A detection effect changes only
the automated detections. Verified or confirmed occasions are therefore
what separates the two.

There are two ways to provide that information:

- **Verified occasions**: detections by an independent method without false
  positives, at some sites (the `verified` table of `fp_data()`).
- **Confirmed occasions**: automated occasions whose detections were
  reviewed and split into true and false observations (the `confirmed`
  argument of `fp_data()`, the observation-confirmation design of Chambert
  et al. 2015). A fully annotated survey confirms every occasion.

Unlike `fp_occu()`, the false-positive intercept is not tied to the
detection intercept by a gap. Detection at an occupied site always exceeds
\(p_{10}\), so the labels of true and false detections cannot switch.

## Fitting and checking

`simulate_fp_rn()` generates data from the model. Here 100 sites with 15
automated occasions each, verified occasions at 30% of the sites, and a
site effect on detection:

```{r simulate, eval = FALSE}
s <- simulate_fp_rn(nsite = 100, nocc = 15, psi = 0.6, b1 = 0.5, r = 0.3,
                    p10 = 0.05, sigma_r = 1, sigma_lam = 0.5,
                    frac_verified = 0.3, nver = 3, seed = 1)
```

The fit with both site effects:

```{r fit, eval = FALSE}
m <- fp_occu_rn(s$data, occ = ~ x, random_det = TRUE, random_abund = TRUE,
                n_max = 25, adapt_delta = 0.99, iter_warmup = 1500,
                iter_sampling = 1500, seed = 1)
m
```

Three choices in this call matter more than in `fp_occu()`:

- `n_max` must be large enough that the Poisson mass above it is negligible
  at every site. The fit warns when it is not, from the derived quantity
  `p_above_nmax`. The cost of the fit grows with `n_max`.
- `adapt_delta = 0.99` avoids most divergences. The site effects create
  funnels, and at the default of 0.95 divergences appeared in most designs
  of the simulations below.
- With many sites, the standard deviations of the site effects mix slowly.
  At 100 sites, 1000 + 1000 iterations left a largest R-hat of 1.01-1.03 in
  half or more of the simulated fits. Longer chains are the remedy.

Before the estimates, check convergence (R-hat, bulk ESS and divergences in
`m$diagnostics`) and the fit to the data:

```{r check, eval = FALSE}
fp_ppc(m)                        # automated detections per site
fp_ppc(m, method = "verified")   # verified detections per site
```

`fp_sites()` gives, for each site, the posterior probability that it is
occupied and its expected abundance given its data:

```{r sites, eval = FALSE}
head(fp_sites(m))   # occupied, abundance, abundance_lower, abundance_upper, ...
```

`loo()` estimates the leave-one-site-out predictive density, with the site
effects integrated out of each site's likelihood. Without that integration
most sites get high Pareto \(k\). The comparison of interest is usually a
model with and without the detection effect:

```{r loo, eval = FALSE}
m0 <- update(m, random_det = FALSE)
fp_loo_weights(with_det = m, without_det = m0)
```

## Calibration

Simulation-based calibration (Talts et al. 2018) checks that the program
fits the model the simulator generates. Parameters are drawn from the
priors, data are simulated from them, and the rank of each true value among
the posterior draws should be uniform. Two designs, 500 datasets each, had
50 sites and 10 occasions: design A confirmed every occasion and had no
verified data, and design B confirmed 20% of the occasions and verified 3
occasions at 30% of the sites.

```{r sbc-table, echo = FALSE}
u <- res$sbc
u$p_uniform <- signif(u$p_uniform, 2)
u <- u[order(u$design, u$parameter), c("design", "parameter", "n", "p_uniform", "mean_rank")]
u$mean_rank <- round(u$mean_rank, 1)
knitr::kable(u, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("design", "parameter", "datasets", "p (uniformity)", "mean rank (of 0-100)"))
```

The ranks are close to uniform. The exception is the slope of log
abundance (`beta[2]`) in design A. Its mean rank is 45.8, about 3 standard
errors below 50, and its posterior median lies on average 0.02 above the
true value. With 13 tests, a single p-value of 0.03 can arise by chance, and
the departure is small. Divergences occurred in
`r pct(min(res$sbc_diag$div_any), 1)`-`r pct(max(res$sbc_diag$div_any), 1)`
of the fits.

## Recovery across designs

The general grid crossed the number of sites (25, 50, 100), occasions (10,
20), the annotation scheme, \(\sigma_r\) (0 or 1) and \(\sigma_\lambda\)
(0 or 0.7), with 100 datasets per cell. The annotation schemes were:

- **verified**: 3 verified occasions at 30% of the sites;
- **partial**: the same, plus 20% of automated occasions confirmed;
- **full**: every occasion confirmed, no verified data.

Other values were fixed (\(\psi = 0.6\), slope 0.5, \(r = 0.3\),
\(p_{10} = 0.05\)), and the fits used the default priors. A signal is a
lower 5% bound of `sd_det_site` above 0.1. Where \(\sigma_r = 0\), a signal
is false. Where \(\sigma_r = 1\), it is power.

```{r grid-table, echo = FALSE}
g <- res$grid
g$design <- paste(g$nsite, "x", g$nocc)
lev <- c("25 x 10", "25 x 20", "50 x 10", "50 x 20", "100 x 10", "100 x 20")
tab <- function(sr, sl) {
  x <- g[g$sigma_r == sr & g$sigma_lam == sl, ]
  m <- tapply(x$sr_lo_gt_0.1, list(factor(x$design, lev), x$annotation), mean)
  m[, c("verified", "partial", "full")]
}
out <- data.frame(sites_x_occasions = lev,
                  sapply(as.data.frame(tab(1, 0.7)), pct),
                  sapply(as.data.frame(tab(0, 0.7)), pct))
knitr::kable(out, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("sites x occasions", "power: verified", "partial", "full",
                           "false: verified", "partial", "full"),
             caption = "Signal for a site effect on detection, with sigma_lambda = 0.7.")
```

Three results stand out:

- Power grows with the number of sites and occasions, from about half at 25
  sites and 10 occasions to above 90% at 100 sites and 20 occasions.
- Beyond the smallest design, the annotation scheme matters little.
  Verifying 30% of the sites gave about the same power as confirming every
  occasion. At 25 sites and 10 occasions without variation in abundance,
  verified data alone gave less power (41%) than partial confirmation
  (54%).
- Variation in abundance raises the false signal only moderately. Without it
  (\(\sigma_\lambda = 0\)) the false signal was
  `r rng(g$sr_lo_gt_0.1[g$sigma_r == 0 & g$sigma_lam == 0])`; with
  \(\sigma_\lambda = 0.7\) it was
  `r rng(g$sr_lo_gt_0.1[g$sigma_r == 0 & g$sigma_lam == 0.7])`.

The other quantities were well recovered. The 90% intervals covered the
true value in `r rng(g$p10_cover)` of the fits for \(p_{10}\),
`r rng(g$r_cover)` for \(r\) and `r rng(g$psi_cover)` for \(\psi\). The
standard deviation of abundance was weakly identified. When it was 0, its
posterior median was `r round(min(g$sl_bias[g$sigma_lam == 0]), 2)`-`r round(max(g$sl_bias[g$sigma_lam == 0]), 2)`,
the scale of its prior.

## Few sites and the prior

A second grid had 21 sites with 11-19 occasions, every occasion confirmed
and no verified data, at three occupancy levels. Each dataset was fitted
under four priors on `sd_det_site`: half-Normal with scale 0.5, 1 (the
default) and 2, and half-Student-t with 3 degrees of freedom.

```{r small-table, echo = FALSE}
a <- res$small
a <- a[a$sigma_r == 0, ]
lab <- c(hn0.5 = "half-Normal(0, 0.5)", hn1 = "half-Normal(0, 1)",
         hn2 = "half-Normal(0, 2)", t3 = "half-t(3, 0, 1)")
sm <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(a, a$prior), function(x) data.frame(
  prior = lab[[x$prior[1]]], false_signal = rng(x$sr_lo_gt_0.1),
  median = paste0(round(min(x$sr_bias), 2), "-", round(max(x$sr_bias), 2)))))
knitr::kable(sm, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("prior on sd_det_site", "false signal", "posterior median"),
             caption = "21 sites, true sd_det_site = 0, over occupancy and p10.")
```

With 21 sites the posterior of `sd_det_site` near 0 follows its prior. The
false signal ranges from almost none under the narrowest prior to above 40%
under the widest. With few sites, report `sd_det_site` under more than one
prior, through `fp_priors(det_site_sd = )`. A signal that holds only under
wide priors is not evidence of variation in detection.

## What the model can and cannot say

- A large `sd_det_site` with many sites is good evidence of variation in
  detection beyond abundance.
- Evidence for the absence of variation in detection needs a large design.
  Where \(\sigma_r = 0\), the Savage-Dickey Bayes factor for
  \(\sigma_r = 0\) exceeded 3 in
  `r rng(g$bf01_gt3[g$sigma_r == 0 & g$nsite == 25 & g$nocc == 10])` of the
  fits at 25 sites and 10 occasions, and in
  `r rng(g$bf01_gt3[g$sigma_r == 0 & g$nsite == 100 & g$nocc == 20])` at 100
  sites and 20 occasions. Variation in abundance lowers these shares. A
  small `sd_det_site` from a small design is not evidence that detection
  does not vary.
- `sd_abund_site` is weakly identified and leans on its prior when the
  variation in abundance is small.
- Abundance in this model is a latent quantity that links detection to
  occupancy. Its scale depends on the assumption that individuals are
  detected independently with the same \(r\). It should not be read as a
  count of animals without independent support.

## References

Chambert, T., Miller, D. A. W. and Nichols, J. D. (2015). Modeling false
positive detections in species occurrence data under different study
designs. *Ecology*, 96, 332-339. https://doi.org/10.1890/14-1507.1

Royle, J. A. and Nichols, J. D. (2003). Estimating abundance from repeated
presence-absence data or point counts. *Ecology*, 84, 777-790.
https://doi.org/10.1890/0012-9658(2003)084[0777:EAFRPA]2.0.CO;2

Talts, S., Betancourt, M., Simpson, D., Vehtari, A. and Gelman, A. (2018).
Validating Bayesian inference algorithms with simulation-based
calibration. arXiv:1804.06788.
